organizations.What they build: German carmaker and Europe's most visible buyer of humanoid robots. After using Figure AI humanoids (Figure 02, then Figure 03 since June 2026) in its US plant Spartanburg, it started Europe's first humanoid pilot in a car plant at Leipzig in 2026 with Hexagon Robotics' wheeled AEON humanoid, delivering parts to the line in battery and component production. Runs a new competence centre for AI + robotics integration.
organizations._relationship_reason: Real industrial use cases and talks on what factories need from humanoids; a sponsor deal is unlikely for a student lab.

organizations.What they build: German carmaker testing Apptronik's Apollo humanoid robots for intralogistics (moving parts and modules to assembly workers) at the Mercedes-Benz Digital Factory Campus in Berlin-Marienfelde. Workers teach the robots by teleoperation and augmented reality (a human remotely drives the robot to record demonstrations). Mercedes also invested in Apptronik.
organizations._relationship_reason: Its teleoperation-based training is the same data-collection idea as LeRobot imitation learning, so a talk or visit is relevant; no student program found.

organizations.What they build: German industrial supplier that is both a humanoid customer and a parts maker. It plans to roll out at least 1,000 Hexagon AEON humanoids in its plants by 2032 and signed a deal (May 2026) to deploy up to 2,000 robots from UK startup Humanoid; it also sells high-precision actuators (the motors+gearboxes inside robot joints) to humanoid makers.
organizations._relationship_reason: Actuator know-how is exactly our weak spot (mechanics); a technical talk or component samples are plausible, large sponsorship is not.

organizations.What they build: Europe's largest online fashion retailer and a major buyer of AI picking robots. Installing up to 50 Nomagic 'Richard' item-picking robots in its European fulfilment centres (2026) and using Sereact dual-arm robots to sort returns at Ceva Logistics sites in Germany and Poland; also invested in Sereact's Series B.
organizations._relationship_reason: Has a corporate venture/tech arm and Berlin tech community; a speaker on real-world picking or a challenge dataset is realistic.

organizations.What they build: German logistics group. Its contract-logistics arm DHL Supply Chain has deployed more than 8,000 robotic systems worldwide (picking, packing, put-away) since its first robotics bet in 2017, and uses SVT Robotics' SOFTBOT platform as one integration layer to plug many robot vendors into its warehouse software.
organizations._relationship_reason: Can explain multi-vendor robot integration at scale (a real software problem fit for 42 students); innovation centres exist but no student program confirmed.

organizations.What they build: UK online-grocery tech company that designs and installs fully robotic warehouses for retailers worldwide: a grid where swarms of 'bots' (more than 17,000 in its sites) fetch storage boxes, plus robotic picking arms. In July 2026 it won a deal to build a robotic warehouse for an unnamed fast-growing European retailer.
organizations._relationship_reason: Large in-house robotics/AI team (swarm control, robotic picking); good for technical talks; UK location limits hands-on access.

organizations.What they build: German automation giant: makes the PLCs, digital-twin and fleet software that factories use to plug robots in (Siemens Xcelerator), and is itself a test customer. In 2025-26 it ran a proof of concept with UK startup Humanoid's wheeled HMND 01 robot moving totes to a conveyor at its Erlangen electronics factory (60 tote moves/hour, 8h+ uptime).
organizations._relationship_reason: Has education/software programs and a Paris presence; plausible for PLC/digital-twin software and a speaker (programs not verified for 2026).

organizations.What they build: European aircraft maker with big French operations (Toulouse). organizations._relationship_reason: French footprint and in-house robotics team make a visit, a talk or a challenge problem plausible.

organizations._relationship_reason: Its sim-to-real controller work with Isaac Sim matches our software strengths; a talk or project brief is realistic.

summary:
1. Demand in Europe is led by carmakers and Tier-1s (BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Schaeffler) piloting humanoids, and by logistics/e-commerce (DHL, Zalando, Ocado, Amazon) scaling picking robots.
2. Integration is dominated by big warehouse integrators (KNAPP, SSI Schäfer, TGW, Swisslog, Vanderlande, Körber) and factory integrators (Comau, Dürr, Siemens), mostly German/Austrian.
3. Money flows from end users buying pilots (Schaeffler: up to 2,000 Humanoid + 1,000 AEON robots; Zalando: up to 50 Nomagic robots) and new 'robots-as-a-service' integrators like Motion (Brussels).
4. Most humanoid hardware in European plants is non-European (Figure, Apptronik, UBTech, Unitree, Hexagon AEON is the exception); the gap is integration, task training and data, which is software work.
5. Best entry point for us: Innov8 (Paris-region Unitree distributor/integrator) for hardware and a joint demo, plus automatica's Robothon challenge and Fraunhofer IPA's humanoid benchmark as public benchmarks to compete on.
